passage:
It was pouring outside the kindergarten, and Hrithik hadn't come today. Asif stood by the window, nose on the glass. At circle time he saved the seat next to him with his hat. "It's for Hrithik."
"He's sick today," the teacher said.
Asif's lip wobbled. At lunch he drew a picture of two boys holding umbrellas. "For Hrithik, tomorrow," he said, and tucked it carefully into his bag.

qa.q: What did Asif use to save the seat?
qa.a: He saved the seat with his hat.

qa.q: What does Asif's lip wobbling suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt sad and missed his friend.

qa.q: How could the teacher support Asif?
qa.a: She could let him make the picture and remind him Hrithik will be back soon.

qa.q: How might Hrithik feel receiving the picture?
qa.a: He would likely feel loved and happy to know Asif missed him. 🙂

grounding: It shows a child missing a chosen friend and showing loyalty.

passage: In their Jaipur colony, Disha always ran to Vinita first at playtime. When the teacher asked them to pick partners, Disha grabbed Vinita's hand. At lunch they swapped rotis. When an older boy teased Vinita about her glasses, Disha stood in front of her. "Stop it. She's my best friend." Vinita held on to Disha's sleeve all the way home.

qa.q: What did an older boy tease Vinita about?
qa.a: He teased her about her glasses.

qa.q: Why did Disha stand in front of Vinita?
qa.a: She felt protective and loyal towards her best friend, so she stood in front of Vinita to stop the teasing.

qa.q: How could a teacher support this friendship?
qa.a: She could praise Disha's kindness and also help the older boy learn not to tease.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel when Disha stands up for her?
qa.a: She likely feels safe and grateful, holding Disha's sleeve all the way home.

grounding: It shows a child preferring a friend and beginning loyalty.

passage:
"Mama, can Parveen come to my birthday?"
"Of course. Who else?"
"Only Parveen. She's my best friend."
"Only one?"
Hrithik nodded. "She gave me her red crayon when mine broke. And she waits for me at the gate."
"What if she can't come?"
"Then I'll save my cake for her."

qa.q: What did Parveen give Hrithik when his crayon broke?
qa.a: She gave him her red crayon.

qa.q: What does Hrithik wanting only Parveen at his birthday show?
qa.a: It shows Hrithik feels fond of Parveen and grateful to her, because she shared her red crayon and waits at the gate.

qa.q: What could Mama suggest to Hrithik?
qa.a: She could suggest inviting a few more friends while making sure Parveen feels special.

qa.q: What would change if Parveen couldn't come?
qa.a: Hrithik would save cake for her, showing his loyalty even when she is away.

grounding: It shows a child's first chosen friendship, preference and loyalty.

passage:
Note from Pallavi, kindergarten teacher, Wednesday:

Vaibhav, five, has a best friend now. He chooses to sit next to the same boy every day and saves him a seat on the mat. Today his friend was absent. Vaibhav asked three times where he was and played alone at the blocks. When another child wanted the friend's seat, he said, "That's his place."

What I did next: I told him his friend would be back soon and helped him join a small group game for today.

qa.q: How many times did Vaibhav ask where his friend was?
qa.a: He asked three times.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav saying "That's his place" suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he feels loyal and protective of his friend's place, guarding their special bond even while the friend is away.

qa.q: How did Pallavi support Vaibhav on a hard day?
qa.a: Pallavi reassured him his friend would return and gently helped him join a group, so he wasn't alone all day.

qa.q: How might the other child feel when Vaibhav refuses the seat?
qa.a: They may feel left out or confused, not knowing how much the seat means to him.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a young child with a chosen friend, missing him and showing early loyalty.

passage:
Arnab, five, and Vikas lived in the same village lane and did everything together: mango picking, chasing hens, sharing a slate.

When Vikas went to his Nani's village for a week, Arnab sat on the step every evening, chin in hands. "When's Vikas back?" he asked his mother.

"Sunday."

He picked the biggest mango from the tree and hid it in the grain tin.

On Sunday Vikas ran up the lane. Arnab dug out the mango. "I saved it for you!" Vikas hugged him.

qa.q: Where did Arnab hide the mango?
qa.a: He hid it in the grain tin.

qa.q: What does Arnab sitting on the step with his chin in his hands suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt lonely and missed Vikas while he was away.

qa.q: How could Arnab's mother support him while he waited?
qa.a: She could help him count the days to Sunday and suggest small things to do, like the mango he saved.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel when Arnab gave him the mango?
qa.a: He felt happy and loved, hugging Arnab because his friend had thought of him.

grounding: Shows a young child in a village missing his chosen friend and showing early loyalty.

passage:
At the kindergarten in Berlin, Selin, five, always sat next to Abebe. They shared crayons and built the same castle every day.
On Tuesday Abebe didn't come. Selin kept looking at the door. She put her coat on his chair so nobody else would sit there.
“He's sick today,” said the teacher.
Selin drew a picture of their castle and wrote an A on it. “For Abebe. Tomorrow.”

qa.q: What did Selin put on Abebe's chair?
qa.a: She put her coat on his chair.

qa.q: How did Selin feel when Abebe didn't come?
qa.a: She missed him and felt a bit sad and worried, looking at the door.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Selin while Abebe is away?
qa.a: The teacher could let her keep the drawing for Abebe and invite her to play with others for a while.

qa.q: How might Abebe feel when he gets the drawing?
qa.a: He would probably feel happy and special that Selin missed him.

grounding: A five-year-old misses her chosen friend and saves his seat when he is absent.

passage:
At the school playground, Binita, five, only wanted to play with Naveen. She saved him a place in the line. She shared her tiffin.
On Friday, an older boy laughed at Naveen's glasses. “Four eyes!”
Binita stepped in front of Naveen. “Stop it! He's my friend.”
The older boy walked away.
Naveen whispered, “Thank you.” Binita held his hand all the way back to class.

qa.q: What did the older boy laugh at?
qa.a: He laughed at Naveen's glasses.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when the older boy laughed at Naveen?
qa.a: She felt angry and protective of her friend.

qa.q: What could a teacher do after the playground moment?
qa.a: A teacher could praise Binita for standing up kindly and speak to the older boy about teasing.

qa.q: How did Naveen feel when Binita stood up for him?
qa.a: He felt grateful and safer, whispering thank you.

grounding: A five-year-old shows loyalty to her chosen friend when he is teased.

passage:
I'm Salma, the neighbour. Last month Joseph's best friend, Kiran, moved to another city. Joseph is five.
For days after, Joseph sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles. He didn't want to play with anyone else.
One evening he asked me, “Aunty, how far is Chennai?”
“Very far.”
He went quiet. Then he said, “I'll draw Kiran a picture so he doesn't forget me.”
Yesterday I saw his mother posting it.

qa.q: Where did Joseph sit after Kiran moved?
qa.a: He sat on the stairs where they used to play marbles.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel after Kiran moved away?
qa.a: He felt sad and lonely, missing his best friend.

qa.q: How could Joseph's family help him with missing Kiran?
qa.a: They could help him send pictures or talk on the phone, and gently invite him to play with other children.

qa.q: How does Salma see Joseph's feelings?
qa.a: Salma notices his sadness and is touched by how he wants Kiran not to forget him.

grounding: A neighbour observes a five-year-old missing his chosen friend and showing loyalty.

passage:
In June, Tarun played with whoever was nearest in the sandpit.
By August, it was always Jatin. They sat together at snack time, swapped biscuits and built one big castle, not two. When another boy took Jatin's spade, Tarun said, "Give it back. It's his."
In September, Jatin was away with a fever for three days. Tarun sat by the sandpit wall and didn't dig. Each morning he saved the spot next to him with his water bottle. "For Jatin."

qa.q: What did Tarun use to save the spot next to him?
qa.a: His water bottle.

qa.q: What was Tarun feeling when he sat by the sandpit wall and didn't dig?
qa.a: Tarun was missing Jatin and felt lonely without his special friend.

qa.q: How could a teacher support Tarun while Jatin is away?
qa.a: A teacher could let Tarun draw a card for Jatin and gently invite him into a small game with others until Jatin returns.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when he comes back and sees his saved spot?
qa.a: Jatin would likely feel happy and wanted, knowing Tarun missed him.

grounding: Over months a young child chooses one friend, defends him and misses him when he is away.

passage:
On the last day of summer camp, it was pouring. Only one swing was under the shed, and ten children wanted it.
Harsha got there first. Pema was stuck at the back of the line.
Harsha swung once, then jumped off. "Pema's turn. She's my friend."
The line groaned. The teacher said, "Harsha, you can give your turn if you choose."
Harsha nodded hard.
Pema swung, laughing. Harsha stood in the rain holding Pema's slippers so they wouldn't wash away.

qa.q: How many children wanted the one swing?
qa.a: Ten children.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when giving her turn to Pema?
qa.a: Harsha felt loyal and happy to do something for a special friend, even in the rain.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Harsha be a good friend and fair to others?
qa.a: The teacher could praise Harsha's kindness while making sure the rest of the line still gets their turns in order.

qa.q: How might the other children in line see Harsha's choice?
qa.a: They might feel annoyed or left out, because the turn went to her friend instead of the next in line.

grounding: On a rainy last day of camp a child shows loyalty to her chosen friend.

passage:
During Ganesh Chaturthi, the colony kids were practising a dance in the courtyard. A tall girl pointed at Rekha. "You're too slow. You can't be in it."
Rekha's eyes filled up.
Devika stepped in front of her. "Then I'm not in it either. Rekha's my best friend."
The tall girl shrugged. Devika took Rekha's hand, and they practised the steps by the stairs, slowly, until Rekha got them.
The next evening, they both danced in the front row.

qa.q: Where did Devika and Rekha practise the steps?
qa.a: By the stairs.

qa.q: Why did Devika step in front of Rekha?
qa.a: Devika felt protective and loyal; she didn't want her best friend left out or hurt.

qa.q: What could an adult in the colony do to help after this?
qa.a: An adult could make it clear that everyone can dance and quietly thank Devika for standing by her friend.

qa.q: What is it like for Rekha when Devika says "Then I'm not in it either"?
qa.a: Rekha feels comforted and valued, knowing her friend chose her over the group.

grounding: During Ganesh Chaturthi a young child stands up for her chosen friend.

passage:
"Where's Francis?" Lokesh asked, standing at the gate on the first day after the Christmas break.
"He's sick today," said Mama.
Lokesh, five, dropped his bag. "But he's my best friend."
"You can play with the other children."

qa.q: How does Francis feel when he returns?
qa.a: Francis feels happy and loved, saying he missed Lokesh.

grounding: Shows a young child preferring a best friend, missing him and showing loyalty.

passage:
In November, the Berlin kindergarten was getting ready for the lantern walk. Selin, five, made two paper lanterns instead of one.
"Why two?" asked the teacher.
"One is for Tomas. He's sick. He's my best friend."
She had played only with Tomas all autumn, building the same stick house by the fence. Without him, she sat by it alone.
At home, she asked her mother to call Tomas's mum. "Tell him I'm saving him a lantern and not letting anyone else in our stick house."
Her cousin Deniz laughed. "You're like his guard!"

qa.q: How many paper lanterns did Selin make?
qa.a: She made two paper lanterns.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling while Tomas was away?
qa.a: Selin was missing Tomas and felt lonely, sitting alone by the stick house they built together.

qa.q: How could the teacher help Selin while Tomas is sick?
qa.a: The teacher could gently invite her into a small game with another child, while letting her keep her plan to save the lantern.

qa.q: What is it like for Tomas to hear Selin is saving him a lantern?
qa.a: Tomas would probably feel loved and cheered up, knowing his friend is thinking of him while he's ill.

grounding: Shows a young child choosing a special friend, missing him, and staying loyal while he is away.
